title: On 5 July 2026, the Israeli Cabinet Became the First Elected Government in Israeli History to Publicly Declare It Will Not Recognise a High Court Ruling — over the Channel 13 Broadcast Regulator and a Netanyahu Trial Witness
beat: Israel 5 July 2026 cabinet declaration refusing to recognise High Court of Justice ruling on the Council of the Second Authority — Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi 'drunk with power' formulation vs Justice Minister Yariv Levin co-signed resolution — Channel 13 acquisition regulator with Yifat Ben Hai Segev as chair (prosecution witness in Case 4000 who reversed pre-trial testimony in Netanyahu's favour in 2022) — six council-member resignations 'under heavy pressure from Karhi' documented in court's interim order — Attorney General Gali Baharav Miara finding that Netanyahu's vote for Ben Hai Segev's appointment violated his 2020 conflict-of-interest undertaking — Movement for Quality Government 'criminal conduct' framing — first-time in Israeli history executive-branch open-disobedience-of-judiciary event
narrative:
On Sunday 5 July 2026, the Israeli cabinet issued an unprecedented declaration that it would not respect a ruling of the High Court of Justice. Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi and Justice Minister Yariv Levin co-signed a resolution stating the government 'will not recognize any decisions, approvals, appointments or actions taken by the Council of the Second Authority' as long as the council lacks the explicit two-thirds quorum required by the 1990 Second Authority law. Karhi publicly accused the judges of being 'drunk with power' and declared: 'When the High Court tramples the law, the state will not comply with it.' Opposition Leader Yair Lapid, former prime minister Naftali Bennett, and Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot all denounced the declaration as a constitutional crisis.

The underlying judicial dispute concerns the commercial broadcasting regulator — the Council of the Second Authority — which oversees the Channel 13 acquisition by a consortium of high-tech entrepreneurs led by a prominent government critic. In March 2026, the government appointed Yifat Ben Hai Segev as chair of the council; she is a prosecution witness in Netanyahu's ongoing corruption trial who reversed her pre-trial testimony in favour of the prime minister in 2022. After the High Court froze the council's operations in May pending review, six members of the council resigned 'one after the other — reportedly under heavy pressure from Karhi,' dropping the body below quorum. The High Court ruled in June that the resignations would not count toward the quorum, and the government is now openly refusing to recognise that ruling.

Reuters and the Financial Times both reported the cabinet declaration as the first time in Israeli history that an elected government has openly vowed to disobey a sitting High Court ruling. Attorney General Gali Baharav Miara had previously stated that Netanyahu's vote for Ben Hai Segev's appointment was itself a violation of his 2020 conflict-of-interest agreement not to have dealings with witnesses in his criminal trial. The Movement for Quality Government, an Israeli judicial-reform watchdog that has tracked the executive-judiciary fight since 2023, issued a statement calling the cabinet declaration 'criminal conduct' and noted that 'a government that chooses for itself which rulings to obey and which to violate is trampling the rule of law.'
analysis:
1. The asymmetric-transparency pattern is the load-bearing structural finding. The government is producing on-record declarations about its refusal to comply with a judicial ruling; the High Court has produced a 60-day evidentiary record of its own finding that the council resignations were 'intended solely to thwart prior decisions.' The government's stated justification ('a quorum cannot exist without the explicit minimum established by law') sits next to the court's factual finding (six resignations under ministerial pressure, with sworn affidavits describing pressure from Karhi personally). The procedural-vs-factual split is the documentary-evidence architecture: the government can argue the law, the court has the affidavits, and the Israeli public is being asked to choose which framing controls without a single piece of disputed evidence in between.

2. The Channel 13 buyout layer is the second load-bearing element. The acquiring consortium includes critics of the government; the regulator that would approve the deal is now suspended in defiance of a court order. The 'rule of law' framing is being invoked by both sides — Karhi says the court itself is violating the 1990 law; the Movement for Quality Government says the cabinet declaration 'is criminal conduct.' The structural finding is that the regulatory body whose decisions would have determined whether the Channel 13 acquisition can proceed is now caught in an executive-vs-judiciary standoff, with the government openly stating it will not recognise council actions and the court having ruled the underlying resignations were engineered to produce exactly that outcome.

3. The Ben Hai Segev prosecution-witness status is the third structural layer. A sitting council chair who was a prosecution witness against Netanyahu in Case 4000 (the Bezeq-Walla! gifts case), who reversed her pre-trial testimony in 2022, and whose appointment to the council chair Attorney General Baharav Miara publicly stated violated Netanyahu's 2020 conflict-of-interest undertaking. This means the structural story is not just 'executive vs. judiciary' — it is executive-branch officials accused of installing a conflicted witness into the very regulatory body that would decide whether a politically inconvenient acquisition goes through. The 2020 conflict-of-interest undertaking is documented; the Attorney General's finding is on the public record; the reversal of testimony in 2022 is documented in the District Court transcript.

4. The council-member resignation sequence is the fourth evidentiary layer. Six members resigned 'one after the other — reportedly under heavy pressure from Karhi,' per Reuters and the Financial Times reporting on the cabinet declaration. The High Court's June interim order referenced 'sworn affidavits describing pressure from Karhi personally' — a primary-source evidentiary basis for the court's finding that the resignations were 'intended solely to thwart prior decisions.' The government has not denied that the resignations occurred; the government has argued that the resignations voided the quorum regardless of cause. The court is treating the cause as legally material; the government is treating the result (six members departed, quorum lost) as the only legally material fact.

5. The historical-baseline layer is the fifth. Reuters and the FT both framed the cabinet declaration as the first time in Israeli history that an elected government has openly vowed to disobey a sitting High Court ruling. The Israeli judicial-reform fight since January 2023 has included multiple rounds of legislation, court intervention, and political confrontation — but until 5 July 2026, no sitting cabinet had publicly declared it would not recognise a court order. The 'first time in Israeli history' formulation is the documentary-credibility anchor: it is a comparative historical claim that anchors the present moment against the prior 78 years of executive-judiciary relations.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On 5 July 2026, the Israeli cabinet became the first elected government in Israeli history to publicly declare it will not recognise a High Court of Justice ruling — over the Channel 13 broadcast regulator and a Netanyahu trial witness. Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi 'drunk with power' formulation and Justice Minister Yariv Levin's co-signed resolution form the primary-source refusal; the High Court's June interim order describing six resignations 'under heavy pressure from Karhi' with sworn affidavits forms the court's documented factual finding; Attorney General Gali Baharav Miara's published finding that Netanyahu's vote for Ben Hai Segev's appointment violated his 2020 conflict-of-interest undertaking forms the structural conflict-of-interest layer; the Movement for Quality Government's 'criminal conduct' framing forms the civil-society counter-record. The procedural-vs-factual split is the documentary-credibility architecture: the government argues law (the 1990 quorum requirement), the court has the affidavits (six resignations engineered to fail the quorum), and the Israeli public is being asked to choose between framings without a single piece of disputed evidence. The Ben Hai Segev witness-status — a prosecution witness in Case 4000 who reversed testimony in Netanyahu's favour in 2022, sitting as council chair while Attorney General has stated her appointment violated the prime minister's 2020 conflict-of-interest undertaking — is the load-bearing structural connective tissue between the broadcast-regulator fight and the corruption trial. The 'first time in Israeli history' formulation is the documentary anchor against 78 years of executive-judiciary precedent.
